\chapter{The Endings Before It}
\label{ch:sa-ordinals-older-endings}
\hlchaptermodality{63}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say all ten Sanskrit ordinals, sort them by which of three endings they take, and say why the word for first belongs to none of them.}

Complete SA-R63-all-ten and run prathamaḥ to daśamaḥ, then group the ten by ending and name the one that belongs to no group.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ṣaṣṭhaḥ]{\sk{षष्ठः} (ṣaṣṭhaḥ) — sixth}

\label{lesson:SA-C63-sixth}



\begin{quote}
Four recalls, at four distances.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{daśamaḥ} — \textbf{R1}, two lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{saptamaḥ} — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{apaṭhat} and name the two things that mark a past tense — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{namratā} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{षष्ठः}}
\textbf{\sk{षष्ठः}} (\emph{ṣaṣṭhaḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}sixth\textquotedblright{}.

The last chapter would have predicted \textbf{\sk{षष्टमः}}. That word does not exist.

\begin{cousinweb}
Macdonell prints the join, as he does for every one of these words. For \emph{fifth} he prints \emph{pañca-má}. For \emph{sixth} he prints:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{ṣaṣ-thá}
\end{quote}

Not \textbf{-\sk{म}}. \textbf{-\sk{थ}}.

So \emph{sixth} is not a broken \textbf{-\sk{म}} word. It is a whole word made with a DIFFERENT ending — one you have not met, which is why the last chapter could not have taught it and did not try.

Two things follow, and the second is the useful one:

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item Sanskrit has at least two ordinal endings, not one.
  \item \textbf{-\sk{थ}} is the one the cousins kept. English still says \emph{six-th}, \emph{seven-th}, \emph{ten-th}; Latin says \emph{sextus} and \emph{quartus}. Both endings were inherited — Latin has the other one too, in \emph{septimus} and \emph{decimus} — and each language divided its numbers between them differently.
\end{enumerate}

So \emph{sixth} is not a broken Sanskrit word. It is one of the numbers that stayed on the ending the whole family shares, while \textbf{-\sk{म}} took the rest.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The missing ordinal, and a second ending the family shares.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ṣaṭ}, then \emph{ṣaṣṭhaḥ}
  \item the ending it uses, and the ending it does not — \emph{\textbf{-tha}}, not \emph{\textbf{-ma}}
  \item the English word with the same ending — \emph{sixth}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What ending does \textbf{\sk{षष्ठः}} carry? (\textbf{-\sk{थ}}.) Which of the two endings did English keep? (\textbf{-\sk{थ}} — \emph{six-th}.)

Source: Macdonell, \emph{A Practical Sanskrit Dictionary}, p. 324 (DSAL).
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[caturthaḥ]{\sk{चतुर्थः} (caturthaḥ) — fourth}

\label{lesson:SA-C63-fourth}



\begin{quote}
Four recalls, at four distances.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ṣaṣṭhaḥ} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{aṣṭamaḥ} — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{yaḥ} and name the word it always calls for — \textbf{R3}, thirty-three lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{viśvāsaḥ} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{चतुर्थः}}
\textbf{\sk{चतुर्थः}} (\emph{caturthaḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}fourth\textquotedblright{}.

Macdonell prints it \textbf{katur-thá}. That is the same \textbf{-\sk{थ}} you met one lesson ago.

\begin{cousinweb}
One lesson ago \textbf{\sk{षष्ठः}} was a single odd word. Now it has company:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{number} & \textbf{ordinal} & \textbf{ending} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\sk{चतुर्}} & \textbf{\sk{चतुर्थः}} & \textbf{-\sk{थ}} \\
\textbf{\sk{षट्}} & \textbf{\sk{षष्ठः}} & \textbf{-\sk{थ}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two words with the same ending are not an exception. They are a \textbf{set} — a small one, but a set, and it has its own territory: \textbf{-\sk{थ}} sits at four and at six, and \textbf{-\sk{म}} sits at five and at everything from seven up.

That arrangement is worth pausing on, because it is genuinely strange. The two endings are not divided by size, or by sound, or by anything a learner could guess. They are interleaved: four, then five, then six, and the ending changes at every step.

Latin does the same thing at the same numbers and draws the line in a different place — \emph{quārtus}, \emph{quīntus}, \emph{sextus} all take the \textbf{-t-} ending, and only from \emph{septimus} does Latin switch to \textbf{-m-}. The two languages sorted an inherited pair of endings into different piles.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A second \textbf{-\sk{थ}} word, which turns yesterday's exception into today's pattern.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{catur}, then \emph{caturthaḥ}
  \item the two words that share \textbf{-\sk{थ}} — \emph{caturthaḥ}, \emph{ṣaṣṭhaḥ}
  \item the number between them, and its ending — \emph{pañcamaḥ}, \emph{\textbf{-ma}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two numbers take \textbf{-\sk{थ}}? (\textbf{Four and six}.) What sits between them? (\textbf{Five, with -\sk{म}}.)

Source: Macdonell, \emph{A Practical Sanskrit Dictionary}, p. 91 (DSAL).
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tṛtīyaḥ]{\sk{तृतीयः} (tṛtīyaḥ) — third}

\label{lesson:SA-C63-third}



\begin{quote}
Four recalls, at four distances.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{caturthaḥ} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{navamaḥ} — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{śaknoti} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{saralaḥ} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{तृतीयः}}
\textbf{\sk{तृतीयः}} (\emph{tṛtīyaḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}third\textquotedblright{}.

Neither \textbf{-\sk{म}} nor \textbf{-\sk{थ}}. This is a third ending, and the number under it has moved as well.

\begin{cousinweb}
Macdonell prints it \textbf{tri-tīya}, and the printed form is \textbf{\sk{तृतीयः}}. Two things happened:

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item The ending is \textbf{-\sk{तीय}}, longer than the other two and unlike either.
  \item The \textbf{\sk{इ}} of \textbf{\sk{त्रि}} became \textbf{\sk{ऋ}} — the vowel you learned to read two chapters ago, here doing ordinary work inside an ordinary word.
\end{enumerate}

That second point is why this lesson is worth its place even for a reader who only wanted the vocabulary. \textbf{\sk{ऋ}} arrived in this book as the first letter of \textbf{\sk{ऋतुः}}, a word where it simply is what it is. Here it is the RESULT of something: a vowel that shifted when an ending was put on. The letter has a job, not just a shape.

The English cousin kept the \textbf{-t-} ending instead: \emph{thir-d}, from an older \emph{thrid-}. Latin took the same road with \emph{tertius}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A third ending, and the vocalic \textbf{\sk{ऋ}} caught doing grammar.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tri}, then \emph{tṛtīyaḥ}
  \item the three endings so far — \emph{\textbf{-ma}}, \emph{\textbf{-tha}}, \emph{\textbf{-tīya}}
  \item what happened to the vowel of \emph{tri} — \textbf{it became \emph{ṛ}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What ending does \textbf{\sk{तृतीयः}} carry? (\textbf{-\sk{तीय}}.) Which vowel replaced the \textbf{\sk{इ}} of \textbf{\sk{त्रि}}? (\textbf{\sk{ऋ}}.)

Source: Macdonell, \emph{A Practical Sanskrit Dictionary}, p. 111 (DSAL).
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dvitīyaḥ]{\sk{द्वितीयः} (dvitīyaḥ) — second}

\label{lesson:SA-C63-second}



\begin{quote}
Four recalls, at four distances.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{tṛtīyaḥ} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{daśamaḥ} — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{icchati} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{śvetaḥ} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{द्वितीयः}}
\textbf{\sk{द्वितीयः}} (\emph{dvitīyaḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}second\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{द्वि}} + \textbf{\sk{तीय}}. Macdonell prints it \textbf{dvi-tīya}.

Chapter six gave you the number as \textbf{\sk{द्व}} (\emph{dva}). \textbf{\sk{द्वि}-} is the shape that same word takes when something is built on it. The ordinal uses that shape and adds nothing else.

\begin{cousinweb}
So \textbf{-\sk{तीय}} is not a one-off either:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{number} & \textbf{ordinal} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\sk{द्व}} (\textbf{\sk{द्वि}-}) & \textbf{\sk{द्वितीयः}} \\
\textbf{\sk{त्रि}} & \textbf{\sk{तृतीयः}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two and three take \textbf{-\sk{तीय}}; four and six take \textbf{-\sk{थ}}; five and seven upward take \textbf{-\sk{म}}. Three endings, each with its own numbers, and no way to predict from the number which one it gets.

There is something else worth saying about this one in particular. Chapter six taught you that \textbf{\sk{द्व}} is grammatically DUAL — Sanskrit's own third number, used for exactly two of anything. The ordinal shows no trace of that. \textbf{\sk{द्वितीयः}} is an ordinary singular adjective describing one thing, the second one. Being \emph{second} is not being \emph{two}.

Sanskrit also uses \textbf{\sk{द्वितीयः}} for \textquotedblleft{}a companion\textquotedblright{} — the second person in a pair. Macdonell lists that sense right beside the numeral.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The third ending confirmed as a pair, and one ordinal left.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{dvi}, then \emph{dvitīyaḥ}
  \item the two words that share \textbf{-\sk{तीय}} — \emph{dvitīyaḥ}, \emph{tṛtīyaḥ}
  \item which of the two changed its vowel — \emph{\textbf{tṛtīyaḥ}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which numbers take \textbf{-\sk{तीय}}? (\textbf{Two and three}.) Is \textbf{\sk{द्वितीयः}} a dual word? (\textbf{No} — \textbf{an ordinary singular adjective}.)

Source: Macdonell, \emph{A Practical Sanskrit Dictionary}, p. 128 (DSAL).
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[prathamaḥ]{\sk{प्रथमः} (prathamaḥ) — first}

\label{lesson:SA-C63-first}



\begin{quote}
Four recalls, at four distances.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{dvitīyaḥ} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{pañcamaḥ} — \textbf{R2}, ten lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{mahyam} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{śyāmaḥ} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{प्रथमः}}
\textbf{\sk{प्रथमः}} (\emph{prathamaḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}first\textquotedblright{}.

Look for \textbf{\sk{एक}} in it. There is none — not a letter of it.

\begin{cousinweb}
Macdonell prints this one with a note the other nine do not get:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{pra-thamá} {[}= pra-tama, spv. \emph{foremost}{]}
\end{quote}

Read it in three pieces.

\textbf{\sk{प्र}} (\emph{pra}) is \textquotedblleft{}forward, in front\textquotedblright{}. \textbf{-\sk{तम}} is the ending that makes a superlative — the \emph{most} of something. And \emph{spv.} is Macdonell's abbreviation for exactly that.

So \textbf{\sk{प्रथमः}} is not \emph{one-th}. It is \textbf{foremost} — the most forward thing — and it landed in the ordinal series because that is what being first amounts to, not because anyone built it out of a number.

English did the identical thing on its own road. \emph{First} is the superlative of \emph{fore}: \emph{fore}, \emph{former}, \emph{first}. Two languages, no contact, the same idea: the word for \emph{first} is not counted to, it is a claim about being ahead.

That is why this chapter saved it for last. Every other ordinal in these two chapters answered the question \emph{what happens to the number?} This one answers a different question, and it could only be heard as different once the other nine had answered the first one.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
All ten ordinals, and the knowledge that the tenth one you learned is not built like any of the others.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{prathamaḥ}, then \emph{dvitīyaḥ}
  \item which number is inside \emph{prathamaḥ} — \textbf{none}
  \item what it literally claims — \textbf{foremost}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \textbf{\sk{एक}} anywhere inside \textbf{\sk{प्रथमः}}? (\textbf{No.}) What does the word literally mean? (\textbf{Foremost} — \textbf{\sk{प्र}}, \textquotedblleft{}forward\textquotedblright{}, with a superlative ending.)

Source: Macdonell, \emph{A Practical Sanskrit Dictionary}, p. 178 (DSAL).
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[prathamaḥ · dvitīyaḥ · tṛtīyaḥ …]{All ten, and the three endings that made them}

\label{lesson:SA-R63-all-ten}



\begin{quote}
Four recalls, at four distances, before the run.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{prathamaḥ} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ṣaṣṭhaḥ} — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{mahyaṁ rocate} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{pītaḥ} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all ten in order — \emph{prathamaḥ dvitīyaḥ tṛtīyaḥ caturthaḥ pañcamaḥ ṣaṣṭhaḥ saptamaḥ aṣṭamaḥ navamaḥ daśamaḥ}
  \item the five that share \textbf{-\sk{म}} — \emph{pañcamaḥ saptamaḥ aṣṭamaḥ navamaḥ daśamaḥ}
  \item the two that share \textbf{-\sk{थ}}, and the two that share \textbf{-\sk{तीय}}
  \item the one that shares nothing — \emph{\textbf{prathamaḥ}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Ten ordinals, and they sort into four groups rather than one list. The evidence is not this book's; it is printed in the dictionary, because Macdonell marks the join inside every headword:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{ordinal} & \textbf{Macdonell's join} & \textbf{ending} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\sk{प्रथमः}} & \emph{pra-thamá} {[}= pra-tama, spv.{]}, p. 178 & \textbf{none — a superlative} \\
\textbf{\sk{द्वितीयः}} & \emph{dvi-tīya}, p. 128 & \textbf{-\sk{तीय}} \\
\textbf{\sk{तृतीयः}} & \emph{tri-tīya}, p. 111 & \textbf{-\sk{तीय}} \\
\textbf{\sk{चतुर्थः}} & \emph{katur-thá}, p. 91 & \textbf{-\sk{थ}} \\
\textbf{\sk{पञ्चमः}} & \emph{pañca-má}, p. 149 & \textbf{-\sk{म}} \\
\textbf{\sk{षष्ठः}} & \emph{ṣaṣ-thá}, p. 324 & \textbf{-\sk{थ}} \\
\textbf{\sk{सप्तमः}} & \emph{sapta-má}, p. 335 & \textbf{-\sk{म}} \\
\textbf{\sk{अष्टमः}} & \emph{aṣṭa-má}, p. 33 & \textbf{-\sk{म}} \\
\textbf{\sk{नवमः}} & \emph{nava-má}, p. 137 & \textbf{-\sk{म}} \\
\textbf{\sk{दशमः}} & \emph{daśa-má}, p. 117 & \textbf{-\sk{म}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Read the right-hand column downward and the order these two chapters used stops looking odd. Chapter sixty-two taught the block of five that share one ending. Chapter sixty-three worked outward from the hole that block left, and every step was licensed by the one before it: \textbf{\sk{षष्ठः}} was strange until \textbf{\sk{चतुर्थः}} made it a pair; \textbf{\sk{तृतीयः}} was a third oddity until \textbf{\sk{द्वितीयः}} made it a pair; and \textbf{\sk{प्रथमः}} could only be recognised as a word of a different KIND once nine words of the same kind had gone past.

Numerical order would have taught all four groups in the first four lessons and named none of them.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many endings make the ten ordinals? (\textbf{Three} — \textbf{-\sk{म}}, \textbf{-\sk{थ}}, \textbf{-\sk{तीय}} — \textbf{and one word that uses none of them}.) Which ending has the most numbers? (\textbf{-\sk{म}}, \textbf{with five}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
